c.tagline: Dutch colonial charm meets Amazon gateway on the Suriname River.

taxi.fareNote: Most taxis negotiate a fixed fare before departure rather than using a meter; agree on price upfront, especially from the airport.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

hood_desc: The UNESCO World Heritage colonial core around Independence Square and Fort Zeelandia, with wooden Dutch-colonial mansions on broad avenues; best for first-time visitors wanting to walk to sights.
Paramaribo's riverside promenade lined with bars, restaurants, and river-view terraces on the Suriname River; suits travelers who want nightlife and scenery within steps of their hotel.
A residential/commercial district just south of downtown with local markets and everyday Surinamese life; good for those wanting quieter nights and authentic food away from the tourist strip.
A practical area anchored by the Zorg en Hoop domestic airstrip, convenient for travelers connecting onward to jungle lodges and Amazon eco-resorts.
Quiet, low-cost residential neighborhoods offering the cheapest stays and genuine local immersion, though a taxi is needed to reach most attractions.

water.note: Tap water in Paramaribo itself is treated and generally safe; use bottled water outside the city.

transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash directly to the driver or conductor in Surinamese dollars; there is no rechargeable transit card. Minibuses ("bussies") are privately operated and pay is collected on board.
transit.hours: Roughly 6:00-20:00 with limited service; night travel relies on taxis.
transit.note: No rail or metro system; public buses and shared minibuses serve the city, though most tourists rely on taxis.

bus: Intercity minibuses to Nickerie, Albina, Brownsberg

tip.r: Not obligatory; rounding up or 5-10% at restaurants for good service is appreciated but not expected.

food.name: Roti
food.desc: Hindustani flatbread torn by hand and dipped into curried chicken, potato, long beans and a hard-boiled egg. Suriname's signature plate.

places.name: Roopram Roti
places.note: The best-known roti name in the country; queues at lunchtime say enough.

places.name: Joosje Roti Shop
places.note: Local favourite for generous portions and properly soft dhal-filled roti.

places.name: Rita's Roti Shop
places.note: Wide choice including pumpkin, eggplant and vegetarian fillings.

food.name: Pom
food.desc: Creole party bake of grated pomtajer root with chicken, orange juice and onion, baked until the top caramelises. Sweet, tangy and rich.

places.name: De Gadri
places.note: Riverside Creole kitchen at the fort, a standard address for pom and moksi alesi.

places.name: Zus and Zo
places.note: Relaxed courtyard restaurant near the centre serving Surinamese classics.

places.name: Centrale Markt stalls
places.note: Market cooks sell pom by the slice, especially around weekends and holidays.

food.name: Bami
food.desc: Javanese-Surinamese fried noodles with chicken, cabbage and sweet soy, eaten from a warung with sambal and a piece of fried chicken.

places.name: Warung Pawiro
places.note: Home-cooked feel and one of the most recommended bami plates in town.

places.name: Sarinah
places.note: Repeat visitors rate it for local food at very fair prices.

places.name: Warung Saeri
places.note: Javanese-Surinamese kitchen turning out bami, nasi and bakabana.

food.name: Saoto soup
food.desc: Clear, fragrant chicken broth built at the table with rice, vermicelli, bean sprouts, egg, crisp potato sticks and sambal.

places.name: Warung Saeri
places.note: Saoto is the house dish in this long-running Javanese warung.

places.name: Sarinah
places.note: Dependable saoto with all the crunchy toppings served on the side.

places.name: Warung Pawiro
places.note: Small family warung on the Javanese food strip north of the centre.

food.name: Moksi alesi
food.desc: Creole mixed rice cooked with salted meat, smoked chicken, beans and coconut milk. Everyday one-pot cooking, sold by the portion.

places.name: De Gadri
places.note: Creole standards served under the trees beside the Suriname River.

places.name: Centrale Markt stalls
places.note: Cheapest and most authentic route to Creole rice plates and fried fish.

places.name: Zus and Zo
places.note: Easy sit-down spot mixing Surinamese and international dishes.

food.name: Bakabana
food.desc: Thick slices of ripe plantain deep-fried in batter and dunked in warm peanut sauce, the country's favourite snack at any hour.

places.name: Warung Saeri
places.note: Bakabana comes hot from the fryer with a generous bowl of peanut sauce.

places.name: Sarinah
places.note: Order it as a starter before the saoto or bami arrives.

places.name: Centrale Markt stalls
places.note: Fried snacks sold all morning to shoppers and market traders.

food.name: Dawet
food.desc: Javanese iced drink of coconut milk, palm sugar syrup and green rice-flour jellies, sweet and cooling in the Paramaribo heat.

places.name: Warung Saeri
places.note: Javanese warungs pour dawet alongside the saoto and bami.

places.name: Sarinah
places.note: Sweet iced drinks are part of the standard warung line-up here.

places.name: Centrale Markt stalls
places.note: Market drink stands mix dawet and fruit juices to take away.

food.name: Parbo Bier
food.desc: Suriname's own lager, ordered in the big brown one-litre djogo bottle and shared around the table with small glasses.

places.name: Zus and Zo
places.note: Garden bar and terrace that fills with locals and travellers in the evening.

places.name: De Waag
places.note: Waterfront cafe in the old weigh house, good for a cold djogo at sunset.

places.name: Blauwgrond warungs
places.note: The Javanese food strip is the classic place for beer with a late plate.

landmarks: Historic Inner City of Paramaribo (UNESCO Site)
A UNESCO World Heritage-listed grid of wooden Dutch colonial townhouses blending European architectural traditions with local materials and craftsmanship, unlike anywhere else in South America.
Fort Zeelandia
A 17th-century star fort built by the French and later fortified by the Dutch, now home to the Surinaams Museum, with cannon-lined ramparts overlooking the Suriname River.
Presidential Palace (Presidentieel Paleis)
A grand white colonial mansion facing Independence Square, fronted by manicured gardens and towering royal palm trees, and the ceremonial seat of Suriname's head of state.
Onafhankelijkheidsplein (Independence Square)
The green, palm-lined civic heart of Paramaribo, framed by historic government buildings and a popular gathering spot for locals at sunset.
Saint Peter and Paul Cathedral (Cathedral of Paramaribo)
One of the largest wooden cathedral buildings in the Americas, its twin neo-Gothic spires and intricately carved timber interior make it a must-see architectural marvel.
Neveh Shalom Synagogue and Jamia Masjid Mosque
A famously photogenic pair of neighboring houses of worship, a synagogue and a mosque sharing a parking lot, symbolizing Suriname's remarkable religious tolerance and diversity.
Waterkant
The lively riverside promenade lined with colonial-era warehouses, restaurants, and bars, perfect for watching boats ply the wide Suriname River at golden hour.
Palmentuin (Palm Garden)
A shady, tranquil park of towering royal palms next to Fort Zeelandia, offering a cool escape and one of the city's most iconic green vistas.
Central Market Paramaribo

A bustling riverside market bursting with tropical produce, spices, and Surinamese street food, reflecting the city's rich multicultural mix of Creole, Javanese, Hindustani, and Indigenous influences.
Arya Dewaker Hindu Temple
One of the largest Hindu temples in the Caribbean region, its colorful, ornately decorated exterior stands as a vivid testament to Suriname's large Indo-Surinamese community.

train.note: Suriname has no passenger railway - the old Lawa line into the interior closed decades ago. Arrive by air into Johan Adolf Pengel International Airport, about an hour south of the city, or overland by road and river ferry from Guyana and French Guiana.

intl.to: Georgetown (Guyana) - via the Canawaima ferry at South Drain
intl.op: minibus and shared-car operators — arranged at Paramaribo travel agents

intl.to: Cayenne (French Guiana) - via the Albina/Saint-Laurent river crossing
intl.op: minibus operators — arranged at the Paramaribo bus stands

bus.note: Both overland routes involve a river ferry and a change of vehicle at the border, and both take most of a day - carry your passport and check visa requirements for Guyana and France in advance. Domestically, minibuses run from Paramaribo to Nieuw Nickerie and Albina from informal stands rather than a central terminal.

intl.to: Albina to Saint-Laurent-du-Maroni (French Guiana) - across the Maroni river
intl.op: Suriname-French Guiana ferry and pirogue operators — tickets at the Albina landing

intl.to: South Drain to Moleson Creek (Guyana) - across the Corantijn river
intl.op: Canawaima Ferry Service — tickets at the South Drain terminal

ferry.note: Suriname's two international crossings are both river ferries rather than sea routes, and neither is at Paramaribo itself - Albina is about three hours east and South Drain four hours west. The Canawaima ferry to Guyana runs once or twice a day and immigration is handled at the terminals. At Albina, official ferries alternate with faster informal pirogues; use the official service so you get your stamps.

half.name: Saint-Laurent-du-Maroni
half.blurb: Riverside town in French Guiana known for its colonial penal colony history.
